source.title: EST: Towards Efficient Scaling Laws in Click-Through Rate Prediction via Unified Modeling
source.authors: Mingyang Liu; Yong Bai; Zhang-Ming Chan; Si-Shuo Chen; Xiang-Rong Sheng; Han Zhu; Jian Xu; Xinyang Chen

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some figure and formula formatting is affected by extraction, but the scaling results and their stated fits are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling-law analysis to industrial CTR prediction and reports fitted performance trends, but uses CTR GAUC rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The study reports four scaling fits for EST's ΔGAUC against inference compute and dense parameter count, split by depth and width scaling. Other reported results, including CTR baselines, component ablations, multimodal integration comparisons, and online A/B results, are not rows because they do not test the scaling-law versions measured here.
record.test_reason: The study fits ΔGAUC of its industrial CTR model (EST) to power laws in inference compute and dense parameter count, following Kaplan et al. This is a new setting with a result on the power-law form (V5). It does not measure language-model held-out loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude that EST shows a clear power-law scaling trend in ΔGAUC with model capacity and compute, steeper for depth than width, and that it outperforms baselines offline and online.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales an industrial CTR model and fits ΔGAUC against dense parameter count and inference GFLOPs. It does not measure language-model held-out cross-entropy, training tokens, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted exponents differ between depth and width scaling paths for both compute and parameter count.

fits_no_version.finding: In the CTR model, the power-law exponent is larger for depth scaling than for width scaling: 0.12 vs 0.10 against compute, and 0.14 vs 0.08 against params.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In recommendation transformers, the scaling exponent depends on whether depth or width is scaled.

record.problems: The scaling evidence is for one CTR model and uses ΔGAUC rather than held-out language-model loss. The text does not report uncertainty for the fits or test extrapolation to substantially larger runs.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant scaling-fit results omitted. Non-scaling CTR baselines, ablations, multimodal integration comparisons, and online A/B results are excluded because they do not measure the scaling relationships recorded here.

untested.parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss is measured.
No extrapolation from small fits to much larger runs.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation; training tokens are not scaled against compute.
No comparison of LM loss across shapes at fixed parameter count.

Data scaling is not fitted; the text only says gains are sustained with more data. The metric is ΔGAUC rather than loss, and scale spans only about one order of magnitude. Image/video, repeated-data and fine-tuning regimes are not tested.
No variation of parameter counting, schedule, data or fitting method; no test for bending away from a power law.

record.verdict_notes: The study scales CTR models, not language models; it is listed under V5 only as another training regime or domain. The fits come from few points (depth N=1–6, width d=32–128) over about one decade. The baseline for ΔGAUC is not specified in the scaling section. Sparse embedding parameters are excluded from P.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out language-model pretraining loss or test power-law loss scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute.
It does not fit small runs and report predictions for runs orders of magnitude larger.
It does not find a loss-minimising parameter/token allocation for a fixed training-compute budget, or scale training tokens against compute.
Depth and width are scaling paths, not comparisons of architecture details at a fixed parameter count measuring loss.

The tested setting is CTR prediction with multimodal content signals, not image or video generation or the listed repeated-data, fine-tuning, and transfer regimes. The metric is ΔGAUC, not held-out pretraining loss.
The study measures CTR prediction performance against scale, but does not test downstream-task performance of language models or its relation to language-model pretraining loss.

The study compares depth and width scaling fits, but does not vary parameter-counting conventions, training schedules, data, or fitting methods; it does not test compute-optimal allocations or curves bending away from a power law.

rows.subject: EST
rows.operation_detail: Fit ΔGAUC against inference compute while varying model depth.
rows.note: The text says ΔGAUC improves monotonically and follows a power-law trend. The stated fit is for EST CTR prediction, not language-model loss.
rows.check: Link to V7 removed: different exponents for depth versus width are a scaling-path effect in a CTR model, not a fitting or setup choice of the kind V7 names. The ΔGAUC baseline model is not stated in Section 6.4, and compute spans only one decade (5–50 GFLOPs).

relationships.condition: EST CTR prediction on Taobao data, depth and width scaling, 5–50 GFLOPs and 30M–0.3B dense params
relationships.reason: ΔGAUC rises monotonically and is fitted by power laws in compute and params (r1–r4). The range is only about one decade, the fits have no uncertainty, and the metric is not loss.
relationships.display_finding: ΔGAUC increases monotonically with power-law fits in compute and parameters over about one decade, without reported uncertainty.
